title: Corebridge and Equitable Stockholders Approve Their $22 Billion All-Stock Merger on July 30, With Closing Still Expected by Year-End 2026 Pending Regulators
summary: About 99.96% of votes cast at Corebridge and 97.24% at Equitable favoured the deal in preliminary results; the combined company will use the Equitable name, trade as EQH and be run by Corebridge's Marc Costantini, with regulatory approvals still required.
description:
One of the biggest deals in American life insurance has cleared its shareholder vote. Corebridge Financial and Equitable Holdings announced on July 30, 2026 that their stockholders had approved the all-stock merger agreed in March. The facts below come from the companies' July 30 release, distributed by Business Wire, and from the companies' March 26 announcement as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The July release says the vote results are preliminary until certified, and it does not say whether any regulatory approval has been received, so we cannot say how close the deal is to completion. Amounts are in US dollars.

Start with the vote. The companies said about 99.96% of the votes cast at the Corebridge special meeting and 97.24% of the votes cast at the Equitable meeting were in favour. Those votes represented about 82.14% of Corebridge's outstanding shares and about 85.84% of Equitable's. The results are preliminary and are subject to certification by the inspectors of election, after which the final tally will be filed on Form 8-K. The Securities and Exchange Commission had declared the Form S-4 registration statement, the document that describes the deal to shareholders, effective on June 23, 2026. The shareholder meetings were held on the day of the announcement, according to the release.

Now the terms. The deal was announced on March 26, 2026. It is an all-stock merger in which the companies will form a new parent company. Each Corebridge share will convert into 1.0000 new parent share, and each Equitable share will convert into 1.55516 new parent shares. Based on closing prices on March 25, 2026, the combined company was valued at about $22 billion. Corebridge shareholders will own about 51% of the combined company and Equitable shareholders about 49%. The company will use the Equitable name and brand, will trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker EQH and will be headquartered in Houston, Texas.

Who will run it? Marc Costantini, Corebridge's chief executive, will be president and chief executive of the combined company, and Robin Raju, Equitable's chief financial officer, will be its chief financial officer. According to the July release, Equitable's chief executive, Mark Pearson, will serve as executive chair; the March announcement said both Costantini and Pearson were slated to serve as executive chair, which we read as a staged arrangement without being able to confirm the details. The board will have 14 members, seven designated by each company, with Corebridge's chair Alan Colberg as lead independent director. Nippon Life, a major Corebridge shareholder, had three board representatives who voted for the deal, and it said it expects to remain a long-term strategic investor.

What will the combined business look like? The companies say it will serve more than 12 million customers and have about $1.5 trillion in assets under management and administration. They expect operating earnings of more than $5 billion and cash generation of more than $4 billion, based on 2027 consensus estimates plus run-rate synergies, according to the release's footnotes. They expect pro forma shareholders' equity above $30 billion, excluding accumulated other comprehensive income, and a leverage ratio of 26%. At the end of 2025, Corebridge's life fleet risk-based capital ratio was about 435% and Equitable's combined ratio under the National Association of Insurance Commissioners' formula was about 475%. Those ratios compare an insurer's capital with the amount regulators require, so higher numbers mean more cushion.

The financial promises are as follows. The companies say the deal will be immediately accretive to earnings per share and cash generation, rising to over 10% by the end of 2028, and that adjusted return on equity should exceed 15% by the end of 2027. They expect more than $500 million of annual run-rate expense synergies by the end of 2028, mainly from consolidating functions, information technology systems and vendors, along with revenue, capital and tax benefits. A strategic element involves AllianceBernstein, the asset manager that Equitable majority-owns, which distributes in 21 countries; over time, the combined company expects to move more than $100 billion of Corebridge's general and separate account assets to it. All of these are the companies' own projections and not independent forecasts, and they may not be achieved.

What happens next? The deal still requires regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions, and the companies expect it to close by the end of 2026. State insurance regulators review changes of control of insurers, and they look at how policyholders will be protected. The July release does not say whether any approvals have been received. Both companies also said in March that they expected to defer their 2026 annual meetings.

What does it mean for policyholders and advisers? Existing annuities and policies remain obligations of the insurance subsidiaries that issued them, and the release does not say that any contract terms will change. Customers of either company may see changes in brand and service over time, since the combined company will operate under the Equitable name. For the industry, the merger is a sign of consolidation among retirement providers. This article is a news summary and not investment or insurance advice.
source_name: Corebridge Financial and Equitable Holdings (Business Wire release of July 30, 2026; SEC filing of the March 26, 2026 announcement)

key_points: Stockholders of Corebridge and Equitable approved the merger at special meetings on July 30, 2026; preliminary results show about 99.96% of votes cast at Corebridge and 97.24% at Equitable in favour, representing about 82.14% and 85.84% of outstanding shares.

The all-stock deal, announced on March 26, 2026, values the combined company at about $22 billion; Corebridge holders get about 51% and Equitable holders about 49%, with each Corebridge share converting to 1.0000 and each Equitable share to 1.55516 new parent shares.
The combined company will use the Equitable name, trade on the NYSE as EQH and be headquartered in Houston, with Marc Costantini as President and CEO and Robin Raju as CFO.

It will serve more than 12 million customers with about $1.5 trillion of assets under management and administration, and the companies target more than $500 million of run-rate expense synergies by the end of 2028.

why_it_matters: This is one of the largest life and retirement mergers in years, and it will change who sells annuities and retirement products to millions of Americans. The shareholder vote removes one hurdle, but state insurance regulators still have to approve a deal that moves large amounts of policyholder assets.

title: The FCA's 'Targeted Support' Regime for Pensions and Investments Went Live on April 6, 2026, Letting Firms Make Suggestions to Groups Without Full Advice
summary: Under policy statement PS25/22, firms can now offer 'suggestions designed for groups of consumers with common characteristics'; the FCA Board confirmed the rules on February 26, applications opened on March 2, and the FCA estimates about 23 million consumers are underserved by advice and guidance.
description:
One of the biggest changes to how British consumers are helped with their pensions and investments took effect in April 2026. The Financial Conduct Authority's 'targeted support' regime, set out in policy statement PS25/22, allows firms to give suggestions to groups of customers who share characteristics, without making a personal recommendation to each one. The facts below come from the FCA's own policy statement page. We have not read the full rules in the policy statement, so we describe the regime at the level given on that page. Where we add general background, we say so.

Start with the timeline. The FCA opened a consultation, CP25/17, on June 30, 2025, which closed on August 29, 2025. It published near-final rules on December 11, 2025, and the FCA Board confirmed the rules as final on February 26, 2026. Firms could apply for a targeted support permission from March 2, 2026, and the regime went live on April 6, 2026. Earlier work shaped the policy: the page lists CP24/27 on pensions targeted support reforms and DP23/5, the discussion paper from the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, the joint review by the FCA and HM Treasury of where guidance ends and advice begins.

What is targeted support? The FCA describes it as a framework for the design, delivery and purpose of 'suggestions designed for groups of consumers with common characteristics'. It covers decisions about both pensions and retail investments. The idea is that a firm can look at a group of customers, such as people approaching retirement who hold a lot of cash, or members of a pension scheme who are drawing down their savings quickly, and send them a suggestion about what to consider. This sits between two existing categories. Generic guidance gives information but no suggestion. Regulated advice involves a personal recommendation based on an assessment of the individual's circumstances, which is more expensive for a firm to provide. As general background, not drawn from the page, a firm might suggest a group of customers who are drawing a pension too fast consider a lower withdrawal rate, or tell customers holding large cash balances to consider investing part of it.

Who can offer it? The FCA page lists pensions and investment firms, including fund and wealth managers, platforms and operators of self-invested personal pensions; pension trustees and trust-based schemes; banks and building societies; friendly and mutual societies; financial advice and investment firms; and trade and consultancy bodies. A firm must apply for a targeted support permission, and the FCA offered a pre-application support service, PASS, as well as pre-application meetings through its FCA Connect system. The page does not say how many firms have applied or been authorised since April, so we cannot say how widely the regime is being used.

How big is the gap that the FCA wants to fill? The page says the FCA estimates around 23 million consumers are underserved by the markets for advice and guidance. This is the FCA's own estimate. Earlier reporting on the regime cited other figures, such as the number of adults with large cash savings and the share who take regulated advice, but those are not on the policy statement page and we have not verified them, so we do not repeat them.

There are two practical pieces of the framework that matter for consumers. First, the Government plans secondary legislation so that workplace pension providers can send targeted support communications to members who have not opted out of direct marketing. In other words, the law on marketing may be changed so that messages about a member's pension are not blocked as marketing. Second, in December 2025 the FCA published joint statements with the Financial Ombudsman Service, on how the two bodies will handle future complaints about targeted support, and with the Information Commissioner's Office, on how firms can communicate with consumers under existing direct marketing rules. The statement with the Ombudsman matters because, if a suggestion turns out badly, customers need to know where they can complain.

Other documents on the page include Handbook Notice 138 and the Advice Guidance Boundary Review (Targeted Support) Instrument 2026, which contains the formal rules. As general background, the regime sits alongside the FCA's Consumer Duty, which requires firms to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, although the page does not describe how the two interact.

What should savers do? A suggestion from your pension provider or platform is not a personal recommendation, and it is not tailored to your whole financial situation. It is a pointer based on a characteristic you share with others, such as your age or the size of your pot. Before acting on it, consider whether your own circumstances, such as other pensions, debts, health and tax position, would change the answer, and consider whether you want regulated advice. Keep a record of what you were told and who told you. Providers, for their part, need to be careful that their groups are sensible and their messages clear.

Why does it matter more broadly? Large UK insurers and wealth groups are already treating targeted support as a growth area. Aviva, for example, listed the regime among the sources of opportunity in its October 16 Wealth briefing. Whether it closes the advice gap will depend on how many firms use it and how well the messages help people, which will not be clear for some time. This article is a summary of a regulator's policy statement and is not financial or legal advice.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority (policy statement PS25/22 page)
image_alt: UK financial advice and pensions regulation (illustrative)
key_points: The FCA's targeted support regime, set out in policy statement PS25/22, went live on April 6, 2026, after the FCA Board confirmed the final rules on February 26, 2026.
Targeted support lets firms give 'suggestions designed for groups of consumers with common characteristics' on pensions and retail investments, without a personal recommendation for each individual.

Firms applied for a targeted support permission from March 2, 2026, with a pre-application support service (PASS) available; eligible firms include banks, building societies, platforms, wealth managers, pension trustees and mutuals.
The FCA estimates about 23 million consumers are underserved by the markets for advice and guidance.

The Government plans secondary legislation so workplace pension providers can send targeted support messages to members who have not opted out of direct marketing, and the FCA published joint statements with the Financial Ombudsman Service and the Information Commissioner's Office in December 2025.
why_it_matters: Most people in the UK never see a regulated financial adviser, yet many face big choices about pensions and savings. Targeted support is the regulator's attempt to give them something more useful than generic information without the cost of full advice, so how firms use it will affect many savers.

title: Pen Underwriting Doubles Its SME Cyber Limit to £10 Million, Raises the Incident Response Tower to £1 Million and Brings UK Cyber Claims Handling In-House
summary: Pen Underwriting will double the main limit on its SME cyber policy to £10 million for companies with revenue up to £600 million from 1 July 2026, raise the separate incident response tower from £250,000 to £1 million, cut some excesses by more than half, lift crime sub-limits and move all UK cyber claims handling in-house.
description:
Pen Underwriting, a UK managing general agent that writes cyber insurance for small and medium-sized businesses, has announced a set of changes that double the main policy limit and widen several of the supporting covers. The details in this article come from Pen's announcement dated 8 June 2026. They are a company's description of its own product, and the policy wording, which was not reviewed, will determine what is actually covered.

The headline change

The main limit on Pen's SME cyber policy doubles to £10 million. It applies to companies with revenue of up to £600 million, and to risks that start on or after 1 July 2026. A policy limit is the most the insurer will pay for claims in the policy period, so the change raises the ceiling for the whole programme. The announcement does not say what the previous limit was in so many words, but a doubling to £10 million implies £5 million.

The incident response tower

Alongside the main limit sits an incident response tower, which is a separate pot of money for the immediate costs after an attack, such as forensic investigation, legal advice and public relations support. It sits outside the main limit, which means that spending from it does not reduce the £10 million. Pen is raising this tower from £250,000 to £1 million, a fourfold increase. The point of a separate tower is that a business can pay for specialists in the first hours and days without worrying that those costs will reduce the money available for later losses.

Crime sub-limits

Sub-limits for crime-type losses are also rising. The announcement lists phishing, corporate identity theft and services fraud, and says that sub-limits increase to £100,000 or £250,000. A sub-limit is a cap on a specific type of loss that is lower than the overall limit. Crime losses such as fraudulent payment instructions are frequent for smaller firms, so these figures determine how much of such a loss the policy will repay. Buyers should check which sub-limit applies to which event.

Underwriting, excesses and rates

Pen says it has simplified its underwriting questions, which should make it quicker to get a quote. Excesses, the amount a policyholder pays before the insurer pays, are cut by more than half for certain revenue bands. Rates have been adjusted at the lower revenue end of the range. The announcement does not give the rate changes, and it does not say which bands receive which excess reductions, so the effect on a given business cannot be judged from the release.

Claims in-house

All UK cyber claims handling is being brought in-house. For policyholders, this means that Pen's own claims team handles claims instead of an outsourced administrator. Whether this improves service depends on execution, which the announcement does not evidence. The change builds on six enhancements to the product that Pen announced the previous September.

The company's message

Ian Summerfield, managing director of cyber at Pen, said: "Our mantra in this market is that cyber risk never stands still, so we won't either." The statement positions the changes as part of a continuing process of product development.

How to read the announcement

Four points are worth separating. First, a higher limit matters most for the larger end of the range, such as a company with several hundred million pounds in revenue, whose potential losses from an outage or data breach could be large. Second, the larger incident response tower may be the most practical improvement for small companies, because immediate costs after an attack are often significant relative to a small firm's budget. Third, lower excesses make claims more likely to pay out from the first pound for small losses. Fourth, a company announcing broader cover is also taking on more risk, so buyers should expect underwriters to scrutinise controls such as multi-factor authentication, backups and incident plans. That last point is a general observation about the market and not something stated in the release.

What buyers should do

A business considering the policy should compare it with others on the same terms, including exclusions for war and infrastructure failure, conditions on security controls, and the definition of business interruption. Broker advice is useful because wordings differ. The announcement is a summary, and the actual cover is set by the policy document.

Putting the limits in context

A £10 million limit for companies with up to £600 million of revenue is a large amount for the SME segment, where policy limits of a few million pounds are common. Whether a business needs that much depends on its size, the data it holds and how reliant it is on its systems. A firm with £600 million of revenue could lose a good deal of income from a prolonged outage, so a higher limit may be appropriate, while a firm with a few million pounds of revenue may find the incident response tower and the crime sub-limits more relevant than the headline figure. The incident response allowance of £1 million is worth noting because it sits outside the main limit, which means that, on the announced terms, the total available for a major event can be higher than £10 million. This last point is simple addition of the two announced figures and depends on the policy wording.

The in-house claims change is also significant for brokers. Having claims handled by the insurer's own team can speed decisions and keep one point of contact, but it also concentrates responsibility. Brokers will likely watch how quickly incident response providers are engaged after a notification, since that is when delays are most costly.

Limits

This article is based on a company announcement and has not been independently tested. It is general information, not insurance advice, and it is not a recommendation to buy a particular product.

key_points: The main limit doubles to £10 million for companies with revenue up to £600 million, for risks incepting on or after 1 July 2026.

The incident response tower, which sits outside the main limit, rises from £250,000 to £1 million, and crime sub-limits for phishing, corporate identity theft and services fraud rise to £100,000 or £250,000.
Underwriting questions are simplified, excesses fall by more than half for certain bands, and rates are adjusted at the lower revenue end.
All UK cyber claims handling moves in-house, building on six enhancements announced the previous September.
Ian Summerfield, managing director of cyber, said the company's mantra is that cyber risk never stands still, so it will not either.
why_it_matters: Small and mid-sized firms are often the buyers least able to absorb a cyber incident. A higher limit and a much larger incident response allowance change what a policy can pay for, but buyers should still compare wordings, exclusions and excesses, not only headline limits.

title: US Insurance M&A Steadies at $29.6 Billion in Six Months to May 2026 as Megadeals Drive 97% of Value and AI Uncertainty Weighs on Brokers
summary: PwC counts $29.6 billion of announced US insurance deal value across 191 transactions from December 2025 to May 2026, down from $31.8 billion across 207 deals in the prior half; megadeals made up 97% of value, and PwC expects more P&C activity and selective broker deals in the second half.
description:
Insurance dealmaking in the United States held broadly steady in the first half of 2026, but almost all the value came from a handful of very large transactions. PwC's midyear 2026 insurance deals outlook counts $29.6 billion of announced deal value across 191 disclosed transactions in the six months from December 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026. In the preceding six months, ending November 30, 2025, PwC counted $31.8 billion across 207 deals. So value dipped by about 7% and the number of deals fell by 16 over the period, using PwC's data from S&P Capital IQ. The figures cover the US insurance market.

The striking feature is concentration. PwC's analysis found that megadeals drove 97% of the recent deal value. That means that a small number of large announcements account for nearly everything, while the many smaller transactions add little to the total. PwC lists several of the notable deals. In December 2025, Howard Hughes Holdings acquired Vantage Group Holdings, a Bermuda reinsurer, for $2.1 billion; Willis Towers Watson agreed to buy Newfront Insurance Holdings for $1.45 billion; and The Baldwin Insurance Group acquired Cobbs Allen Capital Holdings for $1.41 billion. In March 2026, Corebridge Financial and Equitable Holdings announced a merger valued at about $22 billion. PwC also notes that Avocet Partners, through EMC Life, and Aquarian Holdings, through Brighthouse Financial, announced life and annuity acquisitions.

PwC explains the drivers differently for each part of the industry. In property and casualty insurance, better profitability resulting from past rate increases and improved underwriting is attracting investors, particularly to specialty carriers, managing general agents (MGAs), fronting carriers and excess and surplus (E&S) lines businesses. An MGA is an intermediary with authority to underwrite on behalf of insurers, and a fronting carrier is an insurer that issues policies and passes the risk to reinsurers or other capital providers. Investors like these models because they can grow with relatively little capital.

In brokerage, the picture is less clear. PwC says AI raises a question over whether new entrants will undercut incumbents or whether incumbents can defend margins. It adds that slowing organic growth and AI uncertainty are lowering distributor valuations, which could squeeze roll-up strategies, where a buyer acquires many small brokers and combines them. Mark Friedman of PwC US is quoted as saying: "After several active deals years, 2026 has seen uncertainty over how AI may disrupt the sector."

Life and annuity companies are another story. PwC says private equity demand for life and annuity platforms remains strong, but sponsors are more selective and are increasingly using reinsurance, sidecars and minority structures rather than buying whole companies. A sidecar is a vehicle financed by outside investors that takes a share of an insurer's risks. These structures give investors exposure to insurance liabilities and assets without taking on all of a company's operations and regulatory obligations. Strategic buyers are also active: Japanese insurers such as Meiji Yasuda and Nippon Life have bought American life businesses in recent years.

PwC's outlook for the second half of 2026 is specific. For insurance carriers, it expects more property and casualty deal activity, with greater scrutiny of how sustainable underwriting results are, and growth in alternative capital structures. Legal-entity life and annuity deal volume is likely to stay limited. For distribution, deal volume may moderate as buyers become more selective, MGAs with proven profitability may command mid- to high-teens multiples, and PwC expects more deals in adjacent areas such as warranties, vehicle finance and credit protection.

What do these numbers mean outside the deal room? For policyholders, ownership changes generally do not alter existing contracts, but they can affect service levels, product ranges and, over time, pricing strategies. For employees and customers of brokers, consolidation can bring both investment in technology and pressure for cost savings. For investors, the shift toward minority stakes and reinsurance-based deals suggests a preference for sharing risk without full ownership.

It is worth reading the deal list for what it shows about buyer motives. Two of the named transactions, Willis Towers Watson's purchase of Newfront and Baldwin's purchase of Cobbs Allen, are broker acquisitions, which suggests that large distributors were still buying in the early part of the period even as PwC reports valuation pressure later. Howard Hughes Holdings' purchase of a Bermuda reinsurer reflects the continuing interest in reinsurance platforms that can hold long-term investments. PwC does not draw these conclusions itself in the passages reviewed, so they should be treated as interpretation of the list rather than the firm's own findings. What the data do establish is that the largest transactions span brokerage, specialty property and casualty, reinsurance and life and annuity, so no single segment explains the total.

A few cautions apply. The totals cover announced deal value and depend on how PwC and S&P Capital IQ classify transactions; they do not measure completed deals, and some announced deals may not close. The report's "megadeal" threshold is not given in the material reviewed. The Corebridge-Equitable figure is an announced merger value, not a completed transaction.

The overall message from PwC is of a market that remains active but selective. Profitable specialty insurance and well-run MGAs attract buyers, brokers face valuation uncertainty tied to AI, and life and annuity investors prefer flexible structures. If the second half follows PwC's expectations, the number of large property and casualty transactions could rise, while distribution deals become harder to justify unless profitability is proven.

key_points: PwC counts $29.6 billion of announced deal value across 191 disclosed US insurance transactions between December 1, 2025 and May 31, 2026, versus $31.8 billion across 207 deals in the previous six months.

Megadeals accounted for 97% of recent deal value, including the roughly $22 billion Corebridge-Equitable merger announced in March 2026, Howard Hughes Holdings' $2.1 billion purchase of Vantage Group and Willis Towers Watson's $1.45 billion agreement to buy Newfront.

Property and casualty deals are driven by improved profitability from past rate increases, with investors favouring specialty carriers, MGAs, fronting carriers and excess and surplus lines businesses.
AI uncertainty and slowing organic growth are lowering broker valuations, while private equity is more selective in life and annuity and increasingly uses reinsurance, sidecars and minority stakes.
PwC expects more P&C deal activity in the second half of 2026, limited legal-entity life and annuity deals, and MGAs with proven profitability to command mid- to high-teens multiples.
why_it_matters: Insurance mergers decide who owns the companies that pay claims and manage retirement savings. PwC's data show dealmaking is concentrated in a few very large transactions, that investors are wary of how AI might change brokerage, and where buyers expect to find value next.
